name: Château de Beaucastel Châteauneuf-du-Pape 2019
text:
## Château de Beaucastel Châteauneuf-du-Pape 2019

**The story.** Beaucastel is one of the most famous names in Châteauneuf-du-Pape. It sits at the far northern tip of the appellation, near [Courthézon](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Ch%C3%A2teau+de+Beaucastel,+Courth%C3%A9zon,+France&t=k), where the mistral blows hardest. It is also one of the very few estates that grows all thirteen of the appellation's traditional grape varieties and puts every one of them into its red. The same family has owned it since 1909. Today it is led by Jean-Pierre and François Perrin, the sons of Jacques Perrin, with the fifth generation (Marc, Pierre, Thomas, Cécile, Charles, Matthieu and César) working alongside them. The family also co-founded Tablas Creek in California and partnered on the Miraval rosé in Provence.

**The vineyard and how it's made.** The estate describes about 110 hectares in a single block at the north of the appellation, with the classic Châteauneuf soil: big rounded stones (galets roulés) on the surface, with clay, sand and limestone underneath. The stones soak up the day's heat and give it back to the vines at night. Beaucastel has farmed organically since the mid-20th century, so the old vines have sent their roots deep.

Each variety is picked by hand on its own. Syrah and Mourvèdre ferment in conical wooden vats; the other varieties in concrete and enamelled stoneware vats. After the malolactic fermentation the family blends them, and the wine then spends a year in large old oak casks (foudres) before bottling.

The 2019 blend, from the estate's own sheet: Grenache 30%, Mourvèdre 30%, Syrah 15%, Counoise 10%, Cinsault 5%, and 10% shared among the other eight varieties (Vaccarèse, Terret Noir, Muscardin, Clairette, Picpoul, Picardan, Bourboulenc and Roussanne). That much Mourvèdre is unusual for Châteauneuf, where most wines are mainly Grenache. It is what gives Beaucastel its darker, meatier, longer-lived character. The bottle is 14.5% alcohol.

**The vintage.** 2019 was a scorching year in the southern Rhône. The appellation's own report counts just 158 mm of rain over the growing season (against 530 mm in 2018), and seven days in every ten above 30°C between June and mid-September. A heat wave at the end of June peaked at 44.3°C on 28 June. The berries stayed small, which means less juice but more colour and flavour. A welcome 15 mm of rain on 18 September let the Grenache finish ripening, giving thick skins, deep colour and what the growers called remarkable aromatic purity.

Beaucastel's own note on the year: budbreak was early (start of April), flowering went well, and then the heat set in from late June. The vines held up, helped by herbal teas of chamomile sprayed on the leaves against the heat (see the curious details below). Harvest came at the usual time. The estate points out that years ending in 9 tend to be memorable in Châteauneuf.

**What the critics say for 2019.** Critics put this in the mid-to-high 90s:
- **James Suckling: 97** (March 2022, as listed by JJ Buckley). Lots of ripe damson plum and blackberry, with licorice, candied ginger and baking spice. Very powerful, yet he found it calm rather than loud.
- **Jeb Dunnuck: 96+** (November 2021, quoted on the estate's sheet). Blueberries, violets, peppered beef, leather and spring flowers; elegant and balanced, with just a touch of Beaucastel's wild side. He advised 4 to 5 years in bottle, then two decades of drinking.
- **Decanter: 96** (October 2020, on the estate's sheet). Rich damson and cassis, classic and fresh. Not as deep as the 2016 or 2017, but perfectly balanced and very delicious.
- **Wine Spectator: 96** (on the estate's sheet and at JJ Buckley). A strikingly pure display of cassis, cherry and plum, with leather and dried herbs, an iron backbone and a warm-stone finish. "Built to last."
- **Jeff Leve, The Wine Cellar Insider: 96** (January 2022, checked on his own site). Spicy, meaty, earthy and lush, with depth and lift.
- **Wine Advocate: 95** (May 2022, as listed by JJ Buckley). Dark, plummy and cola-scented, rich and savoury, and reminded the reviewer of the 2007 and 2009. He warned it might close up for a while after release.
- **Vinous: 95** (on the estate's sheet and at JJ Buckley). Cherry, blackberry, licorice, lavender and garrigue, lively rather than heavy, with a very long, spicy finish.
- **Jancis Robinson: 18/20** (November 2020, from cask, on the estate's sheet). Violets, garrigue and black-olive tapenade, fresh and zesty.
- **CellarTracker community: 92.9** (from your CellarTracker list). As often happens, drinkers score it a little lower than the critics.

**How it's drinking now.** In October 2026 the wine is seven years old. Dunnuck's 4 to 5 years have passed, and your CellarTracker list gives a window of 2026 to 2040. So it has just entered its drinking window. The Wine Cellar Insider says Beaucastel is better with 6 to 10 years, and great vintages last 10 to 35 years. If you have one bottle, it's a good time to open it. If you have several, keep some for the 2030s, when the Mourvèdre will have softened and the leather and earth notes will come forward.

One thing to know: Beaucastel is famous for a slightly farmyard, leathery note. Some of it comes from a yeast called Brettanomyces, common in Mourvèdre-rich wines. Many people love it as part of the style; others find it too much. It tends to grow with age.

**Serving.** The estate suggests about 15°C, cooler than room temperature, and decanting if you can. The Wine Cellar Insider suggests 2 to 3 hours in a decanter for young vintages. For a 2019 today, I'd decant it about 2 hours ahead and serve it in a large, rounded glass.

**Food.** The Wine Cellar Insider suggests classic meat dishes: lamb, beef, veal, pork, duck, game, roast chicken, braises, stews, sausages and cassoulet, plus mushrooms and even tuna. My picks: a leg of lamb roasted with garlic and rosemary, duck confit, beef daube, or a wild-mushroom dish. I'd avoid delicate white fish and very spicy food, which would fight with the tannin and the 14.5% alcohol.

**Value and where to buy.** In the latest store lists on this site, ZYN in Calgary has the 2019 at $137, and BC Liquor carries the 2019 only in magnum (1.5 L) at $219.99. BC also has the 2020 at $105.99. In the United States, JJ Buckley sold the 2019 at US$89.94 (now out of stock). For a wine scored 95 to 97 that will keep for decades, that is fair value by fine-wine standards.

**From the history books**
- **The Pope's new castle.** Châteauneuf-du-Pape means "the Pope's new castle". In 1309 Pope Clement V, a former Archbishop of Bordeaux, moved the papacy to Avignon. His successor John XXII drank the wine from the villages to the north, improved the vineyards and built the castle that is now the appellation's symbol. The wine became known as "Vin du Pape".
- **A nobleman's barn.** Beaucastel's own story begins in 1549, when Pierre de Beaucastel bought a barn at Coudoulet, land that still belongs to the estate. In 1687 Louis XIV named a descendant, also Pierre de Beaucastel, "Captain of the Town of Courthézon", in a letter signed by the King and his minister Colbert. Vines are first mentioned for certain in the early 19th century.
- **Phylloxera and a Suez Canal engineer.** When the phylloxera louse wiped out the vineyards in the late 19th century, the owner, Élie Dussaud, sold rather than replant. The Wine Cellar Insider says Dussaud had worked alongside Ferdinand de Lesseps, the builder of the Suez Canal. In 1909 Pierre Tramier bought the estate and replanted it. His son-in-law Pierre Perrin, a scientist, modernised it, and Jacques Perrin led it until 1978.
- **France's first appellation rules.** Before the First World War, much Châteauneuf was shipped to Burgundy as "vin de médecine" to beef up thinner wines. Fraud became so common that in 1923 local growers, led by Baron Pierre Le Roy of Château Fortia, drew up France's first appellation rules. They became law on 15 May 1936, when Châteauneuf was among the first six appellations created. One of the baron's rules: vines could only be planted on land dry enough to grow both lavender and thyme.
- **Into the modern age.** Around 1990 the Perrins founded Tablas Creek in Paso Robles, California, with importer Robert Haas, planting Rhône varieties there. In 2006 they joined Primum Familiae Vini, a small club of great family wine estates. From the 2009 vintage, Beaucastel was one of the first wines outside Bordeaux to be sold through the Bordeaux merchants' network, the "Place de Bordeaux".

**Curious details**
- **Chamomile tea for the vines.** In the 2019 heat wave, Beaucastel sprayed herbal teas of chamomile on the leaves to help the vines cope. The estate credits this, partly, for the vines suffering little from drought.
- **A 20-second hot bath.** According to The Wine Cellar Insider, Beaucastel briefly heats some grapes, mainly Grenache and mostly in difficult years, to about 80°C for around 20 seconds and then cools them to 20°C before fermenting. The aim is to deactivate enzymes that cause oxidation, keeping the fruit fresh. It isn't pasteurisation.
- **Mourvèdre from Bandol.** Much of Beaucastel's Mourvèdre came from cuttings taken at Domaine Tempier in Bandol, the most famous Mourvèdre estate in France.
- **The flying-cigar law.** In 1954 the Châteauneuf council, amid local reports of UFOs, passed a decree banning "flying cigars" from flying over or landing in the commune. It is still in force, and a Californian Rhône-style wine made since 1984, Le Cigare Volant ("flying cigar"), is named after the tale.
- **A cellar to match.** In the 1980s Beaucastel built what was then the largest underground cellar in the Rhône Valley.
